newsitem.title: UK: British stocks seen heading lower Monday.
newsitem.headline: British stocks seen heading lower Monday.

text.p: Britain's blue-chip stocks faced further weakness on Monday as the market absorbed the full impact of last week's historic drop on Wall Street, analysts said.
The FTSE 100 index on Friday posted its largest percentage drop since October 1992, falling 2.5 percent to 4,866 in thin trade on the back of an early sell-off in the U.S.
But the British market closed before the worst of Wall Street action, which was sparked by worries about U.S. corporate earnings and a drop in the dollar.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average eventually tumbled to its second-biggest point loss ever, dropping 247 points, or 3.11 percent, to close at 7,695.
That drop -- though nowhere near the Dow's 22.61 percent plunge in October 1987 -- fuelled fears of a knock-on effect on British shares this week.

"I think market makers will mark the market down reasonably sharply first thing on Monday, probably by another 50 points or so, and then there will be a pause," said Richard Jeffrey, economist at Charterhouse Tilney.

"The market will wait to see whether there's any buying interest at those sorts of levels. If there isn't, I think it will see a secondary markdown, or it might just bounce a little bit and wait for Wall Street to open," he added.
The weekend break may help cushion the market's movements on Monday.

"It's quite often the case that when investors have the weekend to think about things, they don't react as vigorously as they might have done had it been an overnight move," Jeffrey said, adding that Friday's drop was worsened by a lack of institutional buyers.
"What you're seeing is institutions deciding that the market's run far enough for awhile. So they're just standing back from it and watching it," he said.
Analysts were divided over whether Friday's fall marked a temporary consolidation or the beginning of a bear phase in stocks, which recently hit record levels in Britain and the U.S.
Jeffrey said he saw potential for a "short bear market" over the next few months.
"The markets are overvalued, particularly in the UK. It wouldn't surprise me to see the UK market fall back by another 10 percent over the course of the summer and autumn," he said.
But other analysts saw some buying opportunities after the FTSE 100's fall from its all-time high of 5,095.3, which it hit as recently as August 7.
"At 5,100, cash was looking a safer bet, but at these levels, I'll pick up the phone and advise clients to get back into stocks," said Robert Buckland, UK stock strategist at HSBC James Capel.
Buyers were expected to continue to favour second-tier industrial firms over blue chip stocks, a trend that helped push Britain's broader index higher last week.
The FTSE 250 index gained 8.3 points, or 0.18 percent, to 4,698 on Friday -- a gain of nearly 50 points on the week.

"The nervousness in the bigger stocks has not spread to the smaller stocks, which have started to rise. And I think we will see more of the same, with people looking for value amongst the mid-caps," Jeffrey said.
With few British companies due to report earnings this week, the market was focusing on Tuesday's U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meeting, which was expected to result in no change in policy.
Closer to home, all eyes were on July UK retail sales data due on Wednesday.
"If growth is too strong year-on-year, it will raise the question again about whether interest rates have to go up," Jeffrey said.
The average estimate of economists surveyed by Reuters was a 5.4 percent rise in July retail sales on the year.
